lines.text: Ananya, a final-year student, asks a chatbot: is Bengaluru good for freshers? The answer appears one word at a time.
That isn't a style choice. A large language model can only do one thing: predict the next token.
First, her question is cut into tokens: chunks of about three or four characters. Bengaluru might be three.
You pay for every token. And every model has a context window: a limit on how many tokens fit at once.
Now the model reads every token so far, and gives each possible next token a probability.
It picks one, adds it to the end, and the longer text goes straight back in.
Then again. And again. Repeated thousands of times, that one trick is chat, coding and reasoning.
Temperature decides how it picks. At zero, it takes the most likely token every time. Same question, same answer.
Around zero point seven, less likely tokens sometimes win. Ask twice, and you get two different answers.
Now Ananya asks a follow-up: what about salaries there? The chatbot knows what there means. How?
The model remembers nothing. The app sends the whole conversation again, inside the context window, every single time.
And because it predicts plausible text, not true text, it can say something confident and completely wrong.
So here's the line that makes you sound like an engineer: an LLM is stateless. Memory is the app's job.
Next lesson: your first LLM API call in Python.
